708.title: Ganga holds out her son
708.hook: Shantanu finds a dam of arrows on the Ganga, and the river goddess brings him his son: why Hindus call the Ganga mother
708.carry: ganga is a mother, not just a river
708.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small sealed pot or bottle of Ganga jal, water from the Ganga, for pujas, blessings and last rites, and evening Ganga aarti is offered on her banks at Haridwar and Varanasi.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nandini, Vasishtha's cow, a curse he couldn't unsay, and why the eighth son had to live.
screen: `WORDS HE COULDN'T UNSAY.`

segments.voice: The Ganga has gone shallow. Shantanu notices it while he's out hunting, following a wounded deer along the bank. The great river is barely moving, as if something were holding it back. Ganga left him long ago, carrying their baby into the water, and he has ruled alone since then. Now he forgets the deer and goes looking for the reason: what on earth could stop a river?
screen: `THE RIVER HAS GONE SHALLOW.` → `SOMETHING HOLDS IT BACK.` → `WHAT COULD STOP A RIVER?`

segments.voice: By the water he finds a young man, tall and handsome, who has stopped the Ganga's flow with arrows, a dam of them across the current. Shantanu has no idea who this is. The young man clouds the king's senses with a power of illusion, and vanishes. So Shantanu calls on Ganga: show me the child. And she rises from the river in a beautiful form, holding the young man by the hand. This, she tells him, is your eighth son, the one I took with me. The text knows him by two names: Devavrata, and Gangeya, Ganga's son. Stay with that picture, because it's how Hindus have seen this river for centuries. Ganga isn't only water. She's a goddess, and a mother: she rises out of her own current and hands a king his child. Hindus still call her Ganga Ma, Mother Ganga. Pilgrims bathe in her at Haridwar and Varanasi, and every evening priests wave great lamps over her in the Ganga aarti. Many families keep a little sealed pot or bottle of Ganga jal, Ganga water, at home: for pujas, for blessing a new house, for a few drops on the lips of someone who is dying. And many carry a loved one's ashes to her. The teaching under it: in Hinduism the sacred can flow through the world itself, a river you can stand in, and you meet her the way you'd meet a mother, with reverence and love. This son will carry her name all his life. For now, a king who lost eight sons is standing beside one of them, handed back by the river.
screen: `A DAM OF ARROWS.` · `YOUR EIGHTH SON: DEVAVRATA.` · `A GODDESS, AND A MOTHER.` · `GANGA JAL, KEPT AT HOME.` · then, large: `GANGA IS A MOTHER, NOT JUST A RIVER.`

segments.voice: If you keep Ganga jal or any water for puja, pour a little into a cup; if not, ordinary water is fine. Hold it, and breathe in, remembering the river who rose to hand a father his son. Breathe out and sprinkle a drop on your head, the way many Hindus do, with a quiet word of thanks to Ganga Ma. If you don't pray, simply hold the water and thank whatever has carried you this far.
Devavrata. Ganga's son, also called Gangeya, who held the river back with a dam of arrows before his father even knew his name.

709.title: The prince and his gurus
709.hook: Ganga names the teachers her son learned from, starting with the sage who cursed him: why Hindus honor the guru
709.carry: knowledge comes down from guru to student
709.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep Guru Purnima, a full-moon day also called Vyasa Purnima, to honor their teachers, and students of Indian music and dance often touch the teacher's feet before a lesson.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Devavrata, Gangeya, and a river who rose as a mother to hand a king his son. Ganga is a mother, not just a river.
screen: `GANGA IS A MOTHER, NOT JUST A RIVER.`

segments.voice: Vasishtha. Ushanas. Brihaspati. Rama, the son of Jamadagni. That's the list Ganga gives the king. She's standing before Shantanu at the river's edge, holding their grown son by the hand, and before she lets go of him she tells his father what the boy has learned while he was away, and whose learning he holds. It's an extraordinary list. And the first name on it should make us stop.
screen: `A LIST OF TEACHERS.` → `SPOKEN AT THE RIVER'S EDGE.` → `THE FIRST NAME.`

segments.voice: He studied the Vedas, Ganga says, with Vasishtha. That's the sage whose cow was stolen, who cursed the Vasus, and who said the one who took her would live long on earth. The one who took her was Dyu. And Dyu is this young man. So the sage who sentenced him to a human life is the one who taught him how to live it. He knows everything Ushanas knows, the teacher the asuras follow, and everything Brihaspati knows, the teacher of the gods. And he knows every weapon known to Rama, the son of Jamadagni, the warrior sage tradition calls Parashurama. Take him home, she says, and she goes back into the water. Shantanu brings his son to the capital and makes him heir, and the text says the people are glad of him. Notice how Ganga shows the king his son is ready. By naming his teachers. That's one of the oldest ideas in Hinduism: real knowledge isn't something you pick up alone. It comes down from guru to shishya, teacher to student, in an unbroken line called a parampara. Who taught you is part of what you know. That's why students of Indian music and dance still touch their teacher's feet before a lesson, and why many Hindus keep Guru Purnima, a full-moon day for honoring teachers. It's also called Vyasa Purnima, after Vyasa, the sage tradition says composed this very poem. One Vasu stays on earth, carrying the learning of gods and asuras, taught by the sage who cursed him.
screen: `TAUGHT BY THE SAGE WHO CURSED HIM.` · `THE TEACHERS OF GODS AND ASURAS.` · `GURU TO SHISHYA.` · `GURU PURNIMA.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE COMES DOWN FROM GURU TO STUDENT.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu prayers begin by remembering the guru. Bring to mind a teacher you honor: a guru, a parent, whoever first taught you your faith or your craft. If it's your way, bow your head or touch the ground before you. Breathe in and feel what they gave you; breathe out and let a quiet thank you go to them. If you don't pray, simply trace one thing you know back to the person who taught it, and thank them in your heart.
Gangeya. Ganga's son, taught by Vasishtha, Ushanas and Brihaspati, and given every weapon Parashurama knew, before his mother hands him back to his father as heir.

segments.voice: Your line: knowledge comes down from guru to student. Next, a scent on the wind, and a woman with a boat. Until tomorrow.

710.title: The king who said no
710.hook: Shantanu falls for the fisherman's daughter but won't give away his son's crown: kama honored, inside dharma
710.carry: kama is honored, but dharma comes first
710.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often describe four aims of life, dharma, artha, kama and moksha, and teach that love and pleasure are good when they are pursued within dharma.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gangeya, a son taught by the sage who cursed him, brought home as heir. Knowledge comes down from guru to student.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE COMES DOWN FROM GURU TO STUDENT.`

segments.voice: A scent on the wind, sweet and strong, out by the Yamuna River. King Shantanu is walking in the woods along the bank when he catches it, and he can't tell where it comes from. So he follows it. It leads him to the water, and to a young woman with a boat, who ferries travelers across. He asks who she is. She's the daughter of the chief of the fishermen, she says, and she plies this boat at her father's bidding.
screen: `A SCENT BY THE YAMUNA.` → `HE FOLLOWS IT TO THE WATER.` → `THE FISHERMAN'S DAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: Shantanu wants to marry her. He goes to her father and asks. The fisherman doesn't refuse; his daughter must marry someday, and the king is welcome. But there's a condition. Promise me, he says, that the son born of her will be king after you. And Shantanu can't. He already has an heir: Devavrata, Ganga's son, the young man he brought home from the river. To promise the crown to a son not yet born would mean taking it from the son he has. So the king won't agree, and goes home. Back in the capital he can't stop thinking about her. He grows quiet and withdrawn, sunk in thought, the text says, and won't tell anyone why. There's a big Hindu teaching inside that silence. Hinduism names four aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, doing what's right; artha, livelihood and success; kama, love, pleasure and desire; and moksha, freedom. Kama is on the list. Wanting someone isn't a sin here; it's one of the good things a life is for. But kama lives inside dharma, not on top of it. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that in living beings he is the desire that doesn't go against dharma. Shantanu's longing is real, and the text doesn't mock it. But his duty as a father comes first: you don't take a son's crown to get what you want. So he carries both, the dharma and the longing, and lets dharma decide. And the person who will notice first is the son the no was meant to protect.
screen: `THE FISHERMAN'S CONDITION.` · `HE WON'T TAKE HIS SON'S CROWN.` · `FOUR AIMS OF LIFE.` · `KAMA, INSIDE DHARMA.` · then, large: `KAMA IS HONORED, BUT DHARMA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you want right now, honestly, without judging it. Breathe in and name it: in Hindu terms that's kama, and it's allowed. You don't have to decide anything now.

711.title: The son who asked why
711.hook: Devavrata asks his grieving father why, hears half an answer, and quietly finds the rest: pitru devo bhava
711.carry: pitru devo bhava: honor your father as god
711.howItsDone: Many Hindus touch the feet of parents and elders to receive their blessing, and caring for aging parents is treated as a child's sacred duty; retellings hold Bhishma up as an example of it.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: a fisherman's condition, and a king who wanted her but wouldn't give his son's crown away. Kama is honored, but dharma comes first.
screen: `KAMA IS HONORED, BUT DHARMA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Devavrata, the heir, has watched his father grow quiet and pale, sitting lost in thought, and he can't find a reason for it anywhere. The kingdom is at peace, and nothing is missing that he can see. So the son does something that takes a little nerve with a king. He stands before him and asks straight out: everything in the kingdom is going well, so why are you grieving? And Shantanu answers him. Just not completely.
screen: `HIS FATHER HAS GONE QUIET.` → `THE KINGDOM IS AT PEACE.` → `WHY ARE YOU GRIEVING?`

segments.voice: Here is Shantanu's answer, in the text's sense. You are my only son, and the wise say a man with one son is like a man with none. You're a warrior, always among weapons. If you fell in battle, what would become of our line? Every word of it is something the king could mean. But it isn't the whole reason he's grieving, and the text lets us see that. He can't say: I want a woman whose father demands your crown. Devavrata doesn't argue. He goes to someone who would know, an old minister devoted to his father, and asks. And the old man tells him: the fisherman's daughter by the Yamuna, and her father's condition. Now notice what the son doesn't do. He doesn't confront his father, or sulk about a crown he might lose. He starts to think about what he can do for him. Hindu tradition holds Bhishma up for exactly this. The Taittiriya Upanishad gives students lines to carry when they leave their teacher's house. One is for the mother, and the next is pitru devo bhava: let your father be like God to you. Many teachers read it this way: not that a father is always right, but that a parent's well-being is sacred, worth your time, your attention, even your own sacrifice. That's seva, loving service, and it's why in many Hindu homes grown children care for aging parents, touch their feet, and keep them close. Devavrata hears a half answer, and instead of feeling shut out, he goes looking for what his father couldn't say.

712.title: A vow before the elders
712.hook: Devavrata gives up the throne before witnesses: why Hindu vows are spoken aloud, before the family and the sacred fire
712.carry: a sacred vow is spoken before witnesses
712.howItsDone: At a Hindu wedding the couple circle the sacred fire with Agni as witness, and many rites begin with a sankalpa, a solemn intention spoken aloud, naming who is undertaking the rite and why.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: a father's half answer, and a son who found the rest so he could help. Pitru devo bhava, honor your father as God.
screen: `PITRU DEVO BHAVA.`

segments.voice: The heir to the throne comes to a fisherman's door, and he doesn't come alone. Devavrata brings old chiefs of the warrior class with him, elders whose word carries weight. He has come on his father's errand: to ask for the fisherman's daughter as a bride for King Shantanu. The fisherman receives them with honor. And then, politely, carefully, with all those elders listening, he tells the prince exactly what's wrong with the match.
screen: `A PRINCE AT A FISHERMAN'S DOOR.` → `ELDERS AS WITNESSES.` → `WHAT'S WRONG WITH THE MATCH.`

segments.voice: The fisherman starts with praise. This match, he says, is one anyone would want. But there is one fault, and he names it: a rival. Whoever has you as a rival, he tells Devavrata, god or demon, can never live happily for long. That's a bold thing for a fisherman to say to the king's heir, in front of witnesses. In effect: the problem is you. Any grandson of his would grow up in your shadow. And Devavrata doesn't argue. He doesn't ask to be trusted. He answers the problem by removing it. Hear my vow, he says, before all these chiefs. The son born of her will be our king. I give up the throne. The place he gives up is yuvaraja, heir apparent, the one his father gave him when he came home from the river. Notice where he speaks it. Not in private, not to his father, but in a fisherman's house, before elders who can hold him to it. That's how Hindus make a vow that counts. A vow, a vrata, is spoken aloud, before witnesses. At a Hindu wedding the couple walk around the sacred fire, and Agni, the fire, is called the witness, with both families watching. A puja often begins with a sankalpa, a spoken statement of who is doing this and why. Saying it out loud, before others, gives your word a weight it can't have in your head. Devavrata wants that weight. The fisherman listens, and thanks him. Then he says there's one more thing he's worried about.

713.title: The vow that named Bhishma
713.hook: Devavrata vows lifelong brahmacharya and the sky calls him Bhishma: a vow chosen, not forced
713.carry: brahmacharya: a vow chosen, not forced
713.howItsDone: Brahmacharya, celibacy and self-restraint, is the discipline of the student stage of life in Hindu tradition, and many Hindu monks keep it for life. On Bhishma Ashtami, some Hindus offer water (tarpana) for Bhishma, who had no children to do it.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: before the elders, Devavrata gave up the throne. A sacred vow is spoken before witnesses.
screen: `A SACRED VOW IS SPOKEN BEFORE WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: The fisherman is a careful man. He has just heard the heir to the throne give up his crown, in front of witnesses, for a grandson who isn't born yet. He believes him. He says so. And then he keeps thinking, out loud, while the elders listen. You'll keep your word, he says. But you'll have sons one day. Will they keep it? A promise is only as strong as the people who inherit it.
screen: `THE FISHERMAN BELIEVES HIM.` → `BUT WHAT ABOUT YOUR SONS?` → `WHO INHERITS A PROMISE?`

segments.voice: Devavrata answers him before the chiefs. I've already given up the kingdom, he says. Now I'll settle the matter of my children. From today, I take up brahmacharya, a vow of celibacy, for the rest of my life. And then, in the text's sense: even if I die without a son, I'll still reach the heavenly worlds. The fisherman is shaken; the text says the hair on his body stood on end. I give her, he says. And the sky answers. Gods, celestial dancers and sages rain flowers on Devavrata's head and cry out a name: this one is Bhishma. In Ganguli's English the name is glossed with one word: terrible. A vow so hard it's frightening. From now on the story calls him Bhishma, after what he promised. Brahmacharya is a real Hindu discipline. It's the first of the four stages of life, the student years, kept while you learn; and many Hindu monks keep it for life, to give everything to God. Bhishma takes it for his father. The Vasus foretold he'd have no children, and Vasishtha's curse said so too, but here nobody forces it on him. He chooses it, freely, out loud. Hindus still remember that choice. In Hindi, a Bhishma pratigya, a Bhishma vow, means a promise nothing can break. And because he had no children to offer him water after his death, on Bhishma Ashtami many Hindus offer it for him themselves.

714.title: He calls her mother
714.hook: Bhishma calls his father's bride mother and brings her home himself: matru devo bhava
714.carry: matru devo bhava: honor a mother as god
714.howItsDone: Some Hindus address goddesses, elders and respected women as Mata or Ma, mother, a word of honor as well as of kinship.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bhishma's vow of brahmacharya, flowers from the sky, and a new name. A vow chosen, not forced.
screen: `A VOW CHOSEN, NOT FORCED.`

segments.voice: The fisherman has given his consent, before the old chiefs who came with the prince. The flowers have stopped falling. And the young prince turns to the fisherman's daughter, the woman he has just won as a bride for his father, and speaks to her as her son. Mother, he says, get into my chariot, and let's go home. With one word, the vow becomes something you can see.
screen: `ONE WORD: MOTHER.` → `GET INTO MY CHARIOT.` → `LET'S GO HOME.`

segments.voice: He doesn't send her with servants. He helps her into his own chariot and takes her himself, to Hastinapura, the Kuru capital. There he tells his father all of it: the condition, the throne, the vow. The text says the kings who heard what he had done praised it, and said it too: he is truly Bhishma. Now notice that word, mother. An hour ago she was the price of a bargain. She's a fisherman's daughter, close to his own age. With one word he gives her a mother's honor, and steps into a family that will grow around him and never through him. The Taittiriya Upanishad has a line in four parts. Matru devo bhava: let your mother be like God to you. Then father, teacher and guest. This week we've met a teacher, Vasishtha, and a father, Shantanu; today a mother, chosen. In Hinduism, mother is a word of honor before it's anything else. Hindus call the Goddess Ma: Durga Ma, Ganga Ma. Older women are Mataji or Auntie. A new bride often calls her husband's mother Ma or Mummy-ji. The word isn't only about who gave birth to you; it's how you decide to treat someone. Eight days ago in our reading, he was a baby carried off by a river. Today he brings a new mother home to his father, with a whole life of keeping that vow still ahead of him.
